name: Carmenère

lines.s10: Carmenère is Chile's signature red, a lost grape of Bordeaux: dark and soft, with black plum, roasted red pepper and a pinch of paprika.
lines.s20: Carmenère came to Chile from Bordeaux in the 1850s and was grown there as Merlot until 1994. It is a soft, dark red with black plum and blackberry, a streak of roasted pepper and paprika, and gentle tannin.
lines.s45: Carmenère is the grape Bordeaux gave up and Chile kept, grown in the warm valleys of Colchagua and Maipo. It tastes of black plum and blackberry, with roasted red pepper, paprika and a savoury note like soy. It is round and soft, with gentle tannin. It ripens weeks after Merlot, and picked too soon it tastes green. Chile ages it in French oak, while the rare Italian bottles are usually lighter and leafier. Pour it with grilled pork, smoked sausage or anything cooked with peppers. Chile grew it as Merlot for over a century, until a French vine expert told the two apart in 1994.
lines.sale: Carmenère is the red for food with a little heat: soft black plum with its own touch of paprika and roasted pepper. Pour it with the smoked sausage or the grilled pork, where a firmer red would taste bitter.

glass.lead: Black plum and blackberry with roasted red pepper, paprika and a savoury touch of soy, on a round, medium to full body with soft tannin.

ladder.where: The Veneto and Friuli in north east Italy
Colchagua, Peumo in Cachapoal and the floor of the Maipo

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium, tannin medium and soft edged, alcohol medium plus, body medium plus to full.

old.where: North east Italy, in the Veneto and Friuli; a little in Bordeaux
old.glass: Tends to be lighter and leafier: raspberry and red plum with a clear streak of green bell pepper and cut grass, medium body and fresher acidity. The Berici hills of the Veneto tend to give riper, darker wines.
old.cellar: Long grown and bottled as Cabernet Franc, usually for drinking young with little or no new oak; now also labelled under its own name.

new.where: Chile: Colchagua, Cachapoal and Maipo in the Central Valley
new.glass: Typically dark, round and ripe: black plum and blackberry with roasted red pepper, paprika, soy and cocoa, soft tannin and medium acidity. Picked early, it shows green bell pepper and tomato leaf.
new.cellar: Picked late, often into May, then aged in French oak; bottled alone under the grape's name or blended with Cabernet Sauvignon for a firmer frame.

contrast.why: Chile's long, dry autumn lets this late grape hang until its green note fades. North east Italy is cooler and wetter at harvest, so the wine stays leafier. In Bordeaux it set fruit poorly and was not replanted after phylloxera.
contrast.blur: A Chilean wine picked early or from a cool year can be as green as any from Italy, and ripe wines from the Berici hills come close to Chile.
contrast.call: Black plum, paprika, soy and cocoa on a soft, full frame lean Chile; raspberry, cut grass and a lighter, fresher body lean north east Italy.

service.temp: 59 to 63 degrees Fahrenheit, 15 to 17 degrees Celsius: a touch cool, so the fruit stays fresh.
service.decant: Seldom needed for a soft young wine; a firm, oaked blend may open with air after a sample.
service.age: Most are ready on release; the serious wines of Apalta and Peumo keep five to twelve years.

with.dish: Grilled pork chop or pork belly
with.why: soft tannin and ripe plum suit rich pork

with.dish: Lamb with cumin or smoked paprika
with.why: the wine's own paprika note echoes the seasoning

with.dish: Stuffed peppers or a pepper stew
with.why: roasted pepper in the glass meets pepper on the plate
the Chilean match: a savoury filling and a soft red

labels.means: The usual spelling on a Chilean label, without the accent: the same grape.
Two warm sites of central Chile, in Cachapoal and Colchagua, where the grape ripens fully.
In Chile a legal term that asks a little more alcohol than the minimum, not a rank of quality.
A wine of the Veneto, in north east Italy, that names the grape on its label.

guest.a: It is as soft and round as Merlot, and Chile sold it as Merlot for years. Carmenère adds a savoury edge that Merlot lacks: roasted pepper, paprika and a touch of soy.

guest.q: Why does it taste a little of green pepper?
guest.a: The grape carries that note by nature, as its parent Cabernet Franc does. Given a long, warm autumn it ripens into roasted red pepper and paprika; picked too soon it stays green.
Born in Bordeaux, at home in Chile. Bordeaux all but gave it up after the vine pest phylloxera in the nineteenth century; Chile had taken cuttings in the 1850s and kept it.

compare.tell: Merlot has the same soft, plummy body but none of Carmenère's savoury streak: no roasted pepper, paprika or soy.
Cabernet Franc, its parent, is lighter and brighter, with redcurrant, pencil shavings and higher acidity; Carmenère is darker, fuller and softer.
Cabernet Sauvignon is firmer and more drying, with cassis and cedar; Carmenère is softer, with roasted red pepper, paprika and soy.

cards.front: Carmenère: the three dates of its story in Chile?
cards.back: Cuttings came from Bordeaux in the 1850s. A French vine expert told it apart from Merlot on 24 November 1994. Chile entered it in the official register in 1998.

cards.front: Carmenère blind: Chile or north east Italy, what tips it?
cards.back: Black plum, paprika, soy and cocoa on a soft, full frame lean Chile. Raspberry, cut grass and a lighter, fresher body lean the Veneto or Friuli.

cards.front: Why does Carmenère taste green when picked with the Merlot beside it?
cards.back: It ripens weeks after Merlot, often into May in Chile. Picked early it keeps a hard note of green bell pepper, which full ripeness turns to roasted red pepper and paprika.

questions.q: A blind red is ruby and medium in body, with raspberry, red plum, cut grass and green bell pepper, fresh acidity and no mark of new oak. The table agrees it is Carmenère. Which origin fits it?
questions.exp: A lighter, leafy Carmenère with fresh acidity and no new oak tends to mark north east Italy. Colchagua is typically darker and rounder, with black plum, paprika and cocoa from French oak.

questions.q: A guest remembers the Chilean Merlot of the early 1990s as oddly green and leafy, and asks why a bottle today tastes so different. What do you tell him?
opts: Much of it was Carmenère, picked too early
Chile's valleys were cooler in those years
The wines were aged in unseasoned oak
The wines were shipped before they were ready
questions.exp: Until 1994 much Chilean Merlot was Carmenère, which ripens weeks later. Picked with the Merlot it kept a hard green pepper note. The weather and the oak were not the cause.

questions.q: A guest finds the same leafy note of green pepper in a Chinon and in a Chilean Carmenère, and asks whether the two grapes are related. What do you tell her?
opts: Cabernet Franc is a parent of Carmenère
Carmenère is a parent of Cabernet Franc
They are one grape under two names
They are unrelated, and the note comes from oak
questions.exp: Carmenère is a natural offspring of Cabernet Franc, the grape of Chinon, and it shares its parent's note of green pepper. The two are separate grapes, and oak gives no such note.

sources.title: The Oxford Companion to Wine, entries on Carmenère and Cabernet Franc
Decanter: From Bordeaux to Chile, International Carmenère Day
Decanter: The curious case of Carmenère in Italy

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it. TASTE.world reads new and the entry agrees that Chile is where a guest meets the grape. The Old World side is the thin one: north east Italy, where it was long grown and bottled as Cabernet Franc, and a few rows in Bordeaux. A reviewer may judge that a guest seldom meets an Old World Carmenère on a list and prefer the home form, with Chile as home; the plan and the fragment would then change together.

The Codex's records on Carmenère read true and nothing here departs from them. The Codex says the grape two ways: kar-men-AIR on the Chile page and kar-muh-NAIR on the Bordeaux page. The entry takes the Chile page's, since Chile is where a guest meets it.

The Italian style, lighter and leafier with green bell pepper and cut grass, stands on the reference works' account of the Cabernet Franc of the Veneto and Friuli, much of which proved to be Carmenère, and on the trade article read through search. That the Berici hills give riper, darker wines is the trade's account and is hedged with tends; no body of the Veneto was read for it.

The date of 24 November 1994 stands on the trade press read through search, and the registration of 1998 on the Codex's own Chile record. The French ampelographer is living and is not named; nor is the estate where he worked. Grande Vidure, an old Bordeaux name seen on some early Chilean labels, was confirmed and left out for room.

The parentage, Cabernet Franc and Gros Cabernet, is the reading of Wine Grapes and agrees with the Cabernet Franc entry of this chunk. The name's root in carmin, for the crimson of the autumn leaf, was found in two general sources and left out for room. Cabernet Gernischt, the name the grape long went under in China, was left out as a label word a guest here will not meet.

The ladder has two rungs, as TASTE gives the grape a warm climate: north east Italy moderate, central Chile warm. Chile's cooler coast is left off because the Codex teaches that the grape struggles to ripen there.

No Creole dish is given. Smoked sausage gumbo would suit it, but the Merlot entry of this chunk already takes that dish, so the sale names smoked sausage and the food list keeps to pork, lamb, peppers and the Chilean empanada.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after ten fixes over two rounds. The cuttings of the 1850s, the day of 1994, the register of 1998, the Colli Berici rule and the poor fruit set in Bordeaux were confirmed; a question named a second parent the sources do not all agree on, one label promised an oak rule the decree does not show, the ripening gap was given as a figure the sources dispute, and two tells parted the grapes by notes both carry.
changed: lines.s45: while the rare Italian bottles are lighter and leafier now reads while the rare Italian bottles are usually lighter and leafier. The Italian clause was said as a rule; usually hedges it.

questions[2].exp: The explanation named Gros Cabernet as the second parent; the reference works give it, but not every source read agrees, and the question asks only of Cabernet Franc, the parent that is settled.

questions[2].q: A guest finds the same peppery, leafy note in a Chinon and in a Chilean Carmenère now reads A guest finds the same leafy note of green pepper in a Chinon and in a Chilean Carmenère. A peppery, leafy note is heard as black pepper; the shared note is green bell pepper.
glass.notes, oak: Cocoa and dark chocolate are one note written twice; one stays.
compare, the Cabernet Franc tell: The tell gave raspberry to Cabernet Franc, but this entry lists raspberry among Carmenère's own notes; redcurrant, which Carmenère does not carry, takes its place.

labels, Carmenere: The usual spelling on a Chilean label, without the accents: the same grape now reads The usual spelling on a Chilean label, without the accent: the same grape. The name as the plan writes it, Carmenère, carries one accent; a Chilean label drops that one.

labels, Gran Reserva: Decree 464 asks a Gran Reserva for at least one degree of alcohol above the legal minimum and a character of its own. The sources read give an oak rule to Reserva Especial and none confirms one for Gran Reserva, so the label no longer promises one.

cards[2].back: It ripens two to three weeks after Merlot, often into May in Chile now reads It ripens weeks after Merlot, often into May in Chile. Two to three weeks was given as settled; the sources read give two to three, about three, and four to five. Weeks, as the spoken line says, is what they agree on.

questions[1].exp: much Chilean Merlot was Carmenère, which ripens two to three weeks later now reads much Chilean Merlot was Carmenère, which ripens weeks later. The same figure, put right the same way.

compare, the Cabernet Sauvignon tell: The tell gave Carmenère plum as a parting note, and the Cabernet Sauvignon pilot lists black plum on its warm rung. Roasted red pepper, paprika and soy, none of them Cabernet's, now part them.
open: The oak notes hold cocoa and coffee and the profile adds no other; dark chocolate went as cocoa written twice.
